chapter: Cups of coffee as a categorical predictor
summary: If we drag cups of coffee to covariates, it is being treated as a scale variable, and you can also choose to treat it as a categorical variable, because the factors box treats everything as categorical. The chi-squared test is all about quantifying an association between two categorical variables, and that's the last combination of types of variables that we'll see. Just as with ANOVA and the t-test, we can do hypothesis testing with a p-value, but we can also get a grip on the effect size in the data.

We're going to be looking at what the observed data look like on the one hand, and on the other hand, what our null model predicts in terms of these counts. The chi-squared statistic is just another test statistic, in the sense that it tells you the difference between what you see in the data and what you expect under the null hypothesis.

The chi-square distribution is shaped by a degrees of freedom setting, similar to how the t-distribution and the F-distribution have these degrees of freedom. If we have two categorical variables with two categories each, the degrees of freedom becomes 2 minus 1 times 2 minus 1 is 1.

We want independent observations, where every person in your design is only influencing their own observation and not those of the others. The second one is specific to the chi-square test, and that is about the expected counts, and we have no normality assumption to worry about, because we are only working with categorical variables.

I have three questions for you, each with categorical outcomes, and then we're going to do some fun analysis. Do you watch the lectures digitally or live, and I would like to predict this based on your self-assessment of your introversion versus extroversion, and whether you are a cat, dog, or other animal lover.

If you have two categorical variables, you can display the full data with such a table, and we are not summarizing the data in any way. Is there some difference in the proportion of introverted people who watch the lectures live to the extroverted people who watch the lectures live?

If personality type and lecture style are independent, the probability of observing somebody who is extrovert and watches the lectures digitally is equal to just the probability of somebody watching the lectures digitally times the probability of somebody being extrovert. So we take the row total, multiply it by the column total, divide it by n, and then we get the expected counts.

We take the differences between observed and predictions, and that summarizes all these differences between observed and expected under the null. In a 2 by 2 case like we have here, it will always be flipped, so that same residual that we are over-predicting for one group, we are under-predicting with for the other group.

The holy grail of the chi-square test is putting all those numbers into one formula, and then we get a single value, and that is our chi-squared test statistic, 2.38. Is this high or not? Well, we don't really know.

The probability of observing the chi-squared statistic, or more extreme, is around 12%, which is not significant for our default alpha value of 0.005. We fail to reject the null hypothesis, so we cannot conclude that there is an association between somebody's personality traits and their preferred lecture viewing style.

The regular chi-square test has the assumption that your expected cell counts need to be sufficiently high, so in a two by two design, your expected cell counts should not be below 5. If you have more than two groups in your design, you shouldn't have more than 20% of the cells with an expected cell count lower than five.

Just as we could choose the Student t-test or the Welch t-test, here you could also choose the regular chi-squared test or the more robust version, Fisher's exact test, which does not make the assumption about the expected cell counts. None of these cell counts is lower than five, so we are fine using the regular chi-squared test.

The model residuals tell you what your null model has predicted for every cell in the design, so was our null model more wrong in predicting extrovert digital viewers, or was it more wrong in predicting extrovert live viewers? It's the extrovert digital viewers that were deviating the most from what was expected under the null hypothesis.

We get to the effect size for categorical associations, and it is a really cool effect size, but it does take a moment to wrap your head around, I think. There's a couple of probability rules that hold when two events are independent from each other.

If A and B are independent of each other, then the probability of A given B is simply the probability of A. If personality and viewing style are independent from each other, then the probability of somebody preferring the digital lecture if they are an extrovert is the same as the probability of somebody preferring the digital lecture.

The probability of somebody being an extrovert in the sample, the observed proportion, is 0.44. If the variables are independent, the probability of somebody being extrovert if they prefer the live lectures will then also be 0.44.

We have odds of 1.3 in the digital group, and we have 0.58 in the live group. Another way of talking about an association between these two variables is saying that these two odds are different from each other.

The ratio of those odds is called the odds ratio, and that is the effect size of the chi-square test, and if your events are independent, then your odds ratio will be equal to 1. We have observed an odds ratio of 2.25, so that's a bit different from 1.
We can also look at the odds of digital versus live in the extrovert group and then also in the introvert group. If we take the ratio of those odds, we still get exactly that same odds ratio of 2.25.

We saw two main ways that we can analyze an association between categorical variables, the chi-squared test statistic that gives us a hypothesis test with a p-value, and the odds ratio. By default, JASP gives the log of the odds ratio, and the log of 1 equals 0, so the null value, if you look at the log odds ratio, is 0.

We go to the Frequencies module this time, because we have observed frequencies, and we get a table that has the chi-squared test statistic and its corresponding p-value. In the Statistics tab we can include the odds ratio, which is only available for two by two designs.

For the final statistics lecture of SSR, today's topic is going to be Bayesian ANOVA. Especially compared to RMS, we really got very close to how statistics is being done in the real world, we're talking about assumptions, interactions, dependence between predictors, all that sort of stuff.

We've seen the frequentist framework, which is all about asking the question, what happens in the long run to my statistical test, focusing on those type 1 and type 2 error rates. The Bayesian framework also allows you to do inferential statistics, but it uses some different metrics for doing hypothesis testing and for parameter estimation.

We're going to repeat some of the core Bayesian concepts that we need to do inferential statistics, and then apply these to ANOVA, and then of course, I'll show you how to do a Bayesian ANOVA in JASP. Chapters one through six you sort of maybe know from a distant past, and the new chapter for today is chapter 7 about ANOVA.

Many years ago, we did this beer tasting test in our lab, where we gave people 2 cups of beer and they had to say which of the two beers was the alcoholic one. If people are guessing, in other words, they cannot taste the difference between the two beers, we would observe a proportion correct equal to 0.5.

The Bayesian framework is all based on this continuous updating of knowledge, where we start with some prior knowledge. We update our knowledge based on that prediction error, and then tomorrow, if we are ready to learn again, we use our knowledge that we end up today with as our starting knowledge of tomorrow.

We update our model beliefs based on the observed data, and that updating step is completely based on how well every individual value of the parameter predicted the data. Taken together, the prior beliefs with our updated knowledge form our posterior beliefs.

As we see in the Bayesian framework, the labels null model and alternative model are not such a useful distinction, because the Bayesian framework doesn't really distinguish between them. Sarah believes that theta is exactly equal to 0.5, and Paul believes it's really 0.8, and they both go all in on a single value, so we call these point models.

Based on what that model says about the parameter, for instance Sarah claiming that theta equals 0.5, we can use some statistics knowledge to reflect what are going to be likely outcomes if Sarah is the true model. You could even just take the ratio of those two yellow bars, and that ratio of these two yellow bars is exactly the Bayes factor.

Instead of claiming a single value for the parameter, we can also consider models that state multiple values, like Alex's model, which believes that every value of the proportion correct is equally likely. Any model that makes a statement about the parameter value, you can derive a sampling distribution from.

Betty's model puts probability mass on all values between 0.5 and 1, so it is claiming that people do have the ability to distinguish between the alcoholic and non-alcoholic beers. We can still ask this sampling distribution how likely the observed data of eight out of 10 was under this model.

These statements of the models, we can also call these prior distributions, and prior distributions are always probability distributions. The prior distribution needs to match the domain of the parameter, and for a proportion, there's one convenient distribution that follows those criteria, and that's called the beta distribution.
So let's say we observe 8 successes out of 10. We're going to look at the likelihood of the observed data for every value in the model.

The likelihood function is not a probability distribution, that's important for you to know, it maps every value of theta onto a value for the likelihood. The likelihood is just a result of the type of data you are working with, it doesn't depend on what model you are updating with.

The marginal likelihood is a more technical way of saying the average likelihood of the observed data for all values in the model, so the marginal likelihood is influenced by the model. We get a marginal likelihood for Alex of around 0.09, and it quite literally sets the bar for what we consider to be better than average predictions from all the values in the model.

The predictive updating factor that we use from going from prior to posterior is that ratio for every value of theta of the likelihood by the marginal likelihood, and whether it's greater than one is exactly based on whether that value predicted the data better than average. Those values will see a boost in plausibility, and the values that did a worse than average job, 0.55 and lower and 0.95 and higher, will suffer a penalty in plausibility.

You can see that the posterior density is exactly increased for all those values that had a higher than average likelihood. Models that only have a single value don't learn from the data, they're so hyper-convinced that theta is 0.5 that no amount of data is going to change their beliefs.

It's a lot more informative to give interval estimates, because they also reflect some uncertainty, and the credible interval is the Bayesian equivalent of an interval estimate. If Alex's model is the true model, there is a 95% probability that the true value of the proportion is between 0.48 and 0.94.

The marginal likelihood for Alex's model was 0.09, and that's how likely 8 out of 10 is on average under Alex's model, the height of the bar in its sampling distribution. For Betty, the marginal likelihood is around 0.17, and we use exactly those numbers to do model comparison.

We are talking about comparing different models to each other, and you could call one of the models the null model and maybe the other model the alternative model. It's more important to pay some attention to how you translate your research questions into some statistical statement, what would theta be equal to if people cannot taste the difference between the beers?

In that same way that we are updating beliefs about parameter values, we can also update beliefs about which of the two models did a better job in predicting the data. The prior odds tell you how many times more likely your one model is compared to the other model before seeing the data.

The updating factor from prior odds to posterior odds is what we call the Bayes factor, and the Bayes factor is nothing more than the ratio of marginal likelihoods of two models. If we get a BF10 of three, it means that the data are three times more likely under the alternative hypothesis compared to the null hypothesis, and if BF01 is 3, the data are three times more likely under the null.

The marginal likelihood of Sarah's model is 0.04, which by itself is not doing much, and for Alex's model, the marginal likelihood is 0.09. The data are 0.48 times more likely under Sarah's model than under Alex's model, or you can take 1 divided by that, 2.07, and say the data are twice as likely under Alex's model than under Sarah's model.

There exist certain human words you can associate with certain values of the Bayes factor, for instance a Bayes factor between 1 and 3 we consider anecdotal evidence. You don't need to memorize these labels, and if you need to do a Bayes factor hypothesis test, the exam question will tell you which threshold to use.

This lovely representation is the way we represent Bayes factors in JASP, and the extent to which you have evidence in favor of one of the two hypotheses determines the proportion of either tomato sauce or mozzarella. A Bayes factor of 1 means the data are as likely under both models, and with a Bayes factor, you can actually get evidence in favor of the null hypothesis.

The Bayes factor has this more continuous way of assessing a model's performance, rather than adopting this binary view of significance, non-significance. If we have absence of evidence, it means a Bayes factor that is not able to decide between the two models, for instance a Bayes factor of 1.5, that's not very decisive.

Good news for people that like the dummy variables, because they are also used in Bayesian ANOVA, so we can still represent our ANOVA model by means of a regression model. The b1 regression slope indicates the group difference between our two groups, and if b1 equals 0, it indicates no difference between the groups.

We have our null model that has a single spike at 0, because this model is really convinced that the regression coefficient equals 0.
